questions.stem: A gas utility ranks safety risk removed first and customer cost second, with no tolerance. Exactly one plan is best on the first objective. Which plan does the lexicographic solve return?

options.text: A plan that gives up some safety risk removed for a lower customer cost
options.says: Trading by scale is what weights do; with no tolerance the first objective cannot fall at all.

options.text: The plan with the lowest customer cost, whatever safety risk it removes
options.says: A later objective only chooses among plans that tie on the earlier ones; it never overrides them.

options.text: The plan that removes the most safety risk, whatever its customer cost
options.says: Right: with zero tolerance the second objective only breaks exact ties, and here there is none.

options.text: A plan halfway between the most safety risk removed and the lowest cost
options.says: Order is not a weight: on GridCap, NPV then risk returned the NPV plan itself, unchanged.

origin.section: A Lexicographic Order Lets a Later Objective Choose Only Among Plans the Earlier Ones Accept

questions.stem: Pass 1 finds a best NPV of $50,000k, and NPV has a 2% tolerance. Pass 2 returns a plan with NPV $49,400k. What does that tell you?

options.text: The plan breaks the tolerance, since it should give up $1,000k of NPV
options.says: The allowed loss is a ceiling: plans move in whole projects, and the sweep shows plans taking less than allowed.

options.text: The plan is valid, since its floor is $49,000k and it gives up less
options.says: Right: 2% of $50,000k is $1,000k, so the floor is $49,000k; giving up $600k is within it.

options.text: The plan breaks the tolerance, since NPV should stay at $50,000k when first
options.says: That holds only with zero tolerance; a 2% tolerance turns NPV into a floor of $49,000k.

options.text: The plan is valid once an absolute tolerance of $600k is added as well
options.says: Either tolerance is enough on its own; the relative one alone allows $1,000k here.

origin.section: The Allowed Loss Is a Ceiling, and the Plan Moves in Steps

questions.stem: A study uses a 1% NPV tolerance. In the base case the best NPV is $40,000k; in a budget-cut scenario it is $30,000k. How much NPV may the scenario's plan give up?

options.text: Up to $400k, since a tolerance is fixed in dollars once the base case sets it
options.says: That describes an absolute tolerance; a relative one is a share of each scenario's own best.

options.text: Up to $700k, since the scenario adds the NPV it lost to the base allowance
options.says: Nothing adds the lost NPV; the allowed loss is the share times the scenario's best.

options.text: Nothing at all, since a relative tolerance applies only in the base case
options.says: A relative tolerance applies in every scenario; it is recomputed from each one's best.

options.text: Up to $300k, since a relative tolerance is a share of each scenario's own best
options.says: Right: 1% of $30,000k is $300k; the lesson's 85% budget case shows 1% shrinking to $212.6k.

origin.section: A Relative Tolerance Follows the Scenario; an Absolute One Stays Put
